# Abstract

Between the end of the Younger Dryas cold snap around 10000BC and the emergence of literate states in southern Mesopotamia and Upper Egypt around 3200BC, the human population of North Africa, the Near East, Anatolia, Transcaucasia, Iran and Afghanistan grew nearly tenfold, from 1,15M to 10,6M inhabitants. Drawn across 17 ecological catchments and 167.993 habitable grid cells, this chapter reconstructs how Epipalaeolithic foraging bands coalesced into permanent mudbrick villages, domesticated emmer, einkorn, barley, sheep, goats and cattle, and eventually filled the great riverine floodplains. During the Natufian and Pre-Pottery Neolithic A horizons (10000BC to 8500BC), growth was modest, lifting regional numbers from 1,15M to 1,85M by 8000BC as sedentary hamlets took root along the Jordan Valley, the Middle Euphrates and the Zagros foothills. Once mixed cereal-pulse farming and caprine herding matured across Anatolia, Cyprus, the Zagros and the Iranian Plateau, regional population doubled to 3,4M by 6000BC and reached 5,2M in 5000BC. The desiccation of the Sahara and interior Arabia after 5500BC concentrated farmers and herders along the Nile floodplain, the Tigris-Euphrates alluvium and irrigated foothill oases, carrying totals to 7,8M in 4000BC and 10,6M in 3200BC. By that terminal Chalcolithic threshold, the Nile Valley and Delta held 1,7M inhabitants (16% of the domain), the Tigris-Euphrates Basin held 1,59M (15%), Anatolia held 1,38M (13%), the Levantine Corridor held 1,27M (12%) and the Zagros-Susiana-Fars arc held 1,06M (10%). Spatial disaggregation rests on 1.472 Epipalaeolithic-Early Neolithic and 5.657 Late Neolithic-Chalcolithic archaeological sites modelled via metric-isotropic radial distance fields and non-stationary Matérn kriging, anchored by 555 individually evidence-assessed settlements (incorporating NERD, C-Turkey, Palmisano et al. 2021, Titolo and Palmisano 2025 and EES Delta Survey records), 29 historical provinces and 2.629 modern administrative districts [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries; @Palmisano2019Holocene; @Roberts2017Human].



# Background

No part of the Old World offers a longer or sharper record of the shift from mobile foraging to village agriculture than the sweep of land running from the Maghreb Tell and the Nile Valley across the Levant, Anatolia and the Zagros Mountains into the Iranian Plateau and the foothills of the Hindu Kush. At the opening of the Holocene around 10000BC, the region was sparsely inhabited by hunter-gatherer and fisher-forager groups recovering from the Younger Dryas cold and dry interval (c. 10900BC to 9700BC), when cool steppe conditions narrowed wild woodland stands across the eastern Mediterranean [@Roberts2017Human; @Borrell2015Synchronou]. Seven millennia later, on the eve of the Early Bronze Age and the First Dynasty of Egypt around 3200BC, walled mudbrick towns exceeding 22k inhabitants at Uruk and 15,9k at Tell Brak stood beside canal-fed barley fields in Mesopotamia, dense predynastic farming villages lined the Nile from Aswan to the Delta and copper-smelting oasis settlements linked western Iran with Bactria and the Helmand basin.

Older archaeological syntheses often treated the Neolithic transition as a single rapid wave radiating outward from a narrow Levantine core. Radiocarbon programmes, archaeobotanical flotations and multi-isotope skeletal studies published over the last two decades point to a far more polycentric and protracted process [@Palmisano2019Holocene; @Santana2021Multi; @Finlayson2020Beyond]. In the southern Levant, strontium and oxygen isotope ratios from Natufian and Pre-Pottery Neolithic burials indicate that sedentary aggregation drew primarily on local foraging territories rather than mass long-distance immigration [@Santana2021Multi]. In southeastern Anatolia and the Upper Tigris-Euphrates arc, monumental stone sanctuaries at Göbekli Tepe and Karahan Tepe arose among communities still reliant on wild gazelle hunting and intensive collection of wild cereals before morphological domestication stabilised [@Sweatman2024Representa; @Biltekin2024Exploring]. Parallel experiments in goat management and wild-barley harvesting unfolded simultaneously along the Zagros piedmont, while wet-phase Holocene lakes across the Sahara and northern Arabia sustained lakeside fisher-hunters and early cattle herders thousands of kilometres from the Euphrates [@Crassard2013Beyond; @Alasmari2026Results].

Two environmental shifts governed where population could expand between 10000BC and 3200BC. The first was the Early Holocene Climatic Optimum (roughly 9500BC to 5500BC), when strengthened monsoon circulation and Mediterranean winter cyclones turned much of the Sahara, the Fezzan, the Sinai and the Nefud desert into seasonal savanna dotted with playa lakes [@Roberts2017Human; @Crassard2013Beyond]. Under those wetter conditions, Epipalaeolithic Capsian bands in the Maghreb, Early Neolithic camps in the western Nefud and Jordan's Harra basalt desert, and coastal shell-midden communities along Oman and the Gulf coast multiplied across landscapes that later became hyper-arid [@Maher2012Twenty; @Thuesen2023Nascent; @Alasmari2026Results].

The second shift was the gradual mid-Holocene aridification between 5500BC and 3500BC, punctuated by abrupt centennial dry spells around 6200BC and 4200BC [@Roberts2017Human; @Borrell2015Synchronou]. As Saharan playas shrank and Arabian wadis dried up, pastoralists and semi-sedentary cultivators converged on perennial rivers and spring-fed piedmont alluvial fans. Nowhere was that convergence more decisive than in Egypt and southern Mesopotamia. Along the Nile, communities combining Saharan cattle herding with southwest Asian wheat and barley filled the floodplain and Delta margins from Merimde Beni Salama and Buto down to El-Badari, Naqada and Hierakonpolis. On the Tigris-Euphrates delta, Halaf and Ubaid canal builders converted seasonal marshes into high-yield cereal belts anchored by Eridu, Ur, Uruk and Nippur. By 3200BC, those two alluvial corridors together accounted for 31% of all inhabitants across the 17 catchments.

Across the eastern half of the domain, topography imposed a different settlement rhythm. In central Anatolia, long-lived mudbrick mounds such as Çatalhöyük, Aşıklı Höyük and Canhasan achieved village densities unmatched in Europe, sustained by intensive household cultivation of glume wheats, naked barley, lentils and peas on alluvial fans [@Bogaard2017Agricultur; @Wright2013Domesticat; @Coulardeau2023Sedentaris]. Further east, the Zagros foothills, Susiana, Fars, the Kura-Aras valleys of Transcaucasia, the northern Khorasan piedmont and the Helmand-Bactrian basins supported strings of smaller mounded villages (*tells* and *tepes*) bound together by transhumant pastoralism and long-distance exchange in obsidian, lapis lazuli, turquoise and native copper.

# Methodology

## Three-Regime Partitioning and Pre-Administrative Catchments

Reconstructing population before written fiscal rolls requires an analytical frame that links deep prehistoric site distributions smoothly to historical and modern administrative benchmarks. HANDBOOK partitions the demographic history of North Africa, the Near East, Anatolia, Cyprus, Transcaucasia, Iran and Afghanistan into three regimes across 27 chronological modules: Regime 1 covers pre-administrative prehistoric and Neolithic catchments from 10000BC to 3200BC; Regime 2 spans dynastic, classical, mediaeval and early modern empires from 3200BC to 1920AD; and Regime 3 covers twentieth- and twenty-first-century national censuses through 2026. This opening chapter constitutes the whole of Regime 1, establishing the 10000BC to 3200BC baseline across 17 ecological catchments that cover 167.993 habitable 5-arcminute cells.

Each catchment is defined along hydrographic watersheds, alluvial floodplains and mountain piedmonts rather than arbitrary modern borders. In the west, the Maghreb Tell and Atlas Basins, the Tripolitania and Cyrenaica Coast, Saharan and Fezzan Pluvial Basins and Atlantic Sahara Wadis separate Mediterranean winter-rainfall plains from interior desert playas. Across the eastern Mediterranean and Near East, the Nile Valley, Delta and Western Oases stand apart from the Levantine Corridor and Jordan Valley, Cyprus Catchments, the Anatolian Plateau and Coasts and the Tigris-Euphrates Alluvial Basin. Further east and north, the Zagros Piedmont, Susiana and Fars, the Iranian Plateau and Khorasan, Transcaucasia and the Kura-Aras Basin, the Helmand and Sistan Basin and the Hindu Kush and Bactrian Foothills capture distinct highland-basin complexes, while Yemen and Asir Highlands, Oman, Gulf Coast and Hadramawt, and Interior Arabian Wadis and Nefud divide the Arabian Peninsula by monsoon exposure and coastal access.

## Household Areas, Site Multipliers and Radiocarbon Proxies

Population trajectories for individual excavated settlements and regional catchments combine three independent archaeological estimators: domestic roofed floor area, contemporaneous dwelling counts per phase and cemetery or radiocarbon-activity curves [@BirchChapman2017Estimating; @Kadowaki2012Household; @Palmisano2019Holocene]. At single-period and multi-period villages, residential population scales sub-linearly with total roofed space and compound area. For round semi-subterranean Natufian and PPNA huts at Wadi Faynan 16 (WF16), Nahal Ein Gev II and Shubayqa 6, excavated floor areas of 10 to 22 m² housed nuclear family units of roughly 4 to 5,5 persons [@Grosman2016Nahal; @Finlayson2011Architectu; @Thuesen2023Nascent]. With the PPNB shift to rectangular mudbrick pier-houses and multi-roomed agglutinative compounds at Beidha, 'Ain Ghazal, Ba'ja, Çayönü and Çatalhöyük, residential floor footprints expanded to 25 to 55 m², raising mean household sizes to 5,5 to 7,5 persons once upper-storey storage and courtyard work areas are separated from sleeping quarters [@Balbo2012Squaring; @Kadowaki2012Household; @BirchChapman2017Estimating; @Wright2013Domesticat].

At the regional scale, raw site counts cannot be summed directly because settlement longevity ($\tau_{\text{site}}$) varies sharply between mobile Epipalaeolithic camps, long-lived mudbrick tells and Chalcolithic megasites. For a given catchment $z$ and chronological horizon $t$, regional population is therefore calibrated by discounting total recorded sites $N_z(t)$ by phase overlap and mean contemporaneous village size:

$$P_z(t) = \sum_{k} \hat{N}_{z,k}(t) \cdot \left(\frac{\bar{\tau}_{k}}{\Delta T_t}\right) \cdot \bar{H}_k \cdot \mu_k$$

where $\hat{N}_{z,k}(t)$ is the survey-corrected site count in settlement tier $k$, $\bar{\tau}_k / \Delta T_t$ adjusts for mean occupation duration within horizon window $\Delta T_t$, $\bar{H}_k$ is mean active households per site and $\mu_k$ is mean household size. Where regional excavation coverage is uneven, summed radiocarbon probability distributions and eastern Mediterranean pollen diagrams provide independent relative growth curves that constrain inter-horizon slopes between 10000BC and 3200BC [@Palmisano2019Holocene; @Roberts2017Human; @Borrell2015Synchronou].

## Metric-Isotropic Radial Modelling and Non-Stationary Matérn Kriging

Because archaeological surveys cluster along modern roads, river valleys and research concessions, unadjusted point scatters exaggerate density around excavated tells while leaving inter-valley foothills empty. To turn uneven point inventories into continuous 5-arcminute demographic surfaces across all 167.993 domain cells, HANDBOOK aggregates primary regional registers and monograph excavation tables—excluding global crowd databases—onto scale-adaptive Voronoi catchments built from natural drainage basins and subadministrative boundaries. Across HANDBOOK, the spatial sampling mesh yields a median Voronoi catchment radius of 32,51 km and a 90th-percentile radius of 40,25 km, keeping interpolation distances tight across both Mediterranean valleys and plateau corridors.

Raw site intensities in each catchment undergo a Freeman-Tukey variance-stabilising transformation before spatial regression against biophysical covariates via weighted least squares (WLS). Four environmental predictors capture prehistoric settlement attraction: baseline habitability ($\beta_0$), natural net primary productivity ($\beta_1$), ecological diversity ($\beta_2$), perennial fluvial proximity ($\beta_3$) and coastal access ($\beta_4$). For the Epipalaeolithic and Early Neolithic horizon (1.472 mapped sites across 278 active domestic catchments), fitted WLS parameters register $\beta_0 = 0,1836$, $\beta_1 = 0,01$, $\beta_2 = 0,0348$, $\beta_3 = 0,1099$ and $\beta_4 = 0,0987$. By the Late Neolithic and Chalcolithic horizon (5.657 sites across 1.186 active catchments), the fluvial coefficient remains high ($\beta_3 = 0,1058$) and coastal proximity remains strong ($\beta_4 = 0,0907$), while baseline background habitability drops to $\beta_0 = 0,0782$ as communities concentrate more tightly onto irrigable valleys and alluvial fans.

Residuals from the WLS trend surface are interpolated across a metric-isotropic geodesic radial distance field $u_{ij} = d_{ij} / r_{ij}$ normalised by local catchment radius, using a non-stationary two-component Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) semivariogram:

$$\gamma(u) = c_0 + (1 - c_0)\left[1 - c_1\left(1 + \frac{\sqrt{3}\,u}{\tau_1}\right)e^{-\sqrt{3}\,u/\tau_1} - c_2\left(1 + \frac{\sqrt{3}\,u}{\tau_2}\right)e^{-\sqrt{3}\,u/\tau_2}\right]$$

with weights $c_1 = 0,8$, $c_2 = 0,2$, nugget-to-sill ratio $c_0 = 0,04$, dimensionless short range $\tau_1 = 1,35$ (raw empirical fits of $1,49$ in the Early Neolithic and $1,53$ in the Late Neolithic-Chalcolithic, corresponding to effective short-range correlation lengths of 48,29 km and 49,71 km) and secondary range $\tau_2 = 2,90$. Empirical semivariogram fits attain $R^2 = 0,999$ across both prehistoric horizons, ensuring smooth continuous surfaces that fade cleanly across arid desert barriers without bleeding urban halos into hyper-arid basins.

## Subadministrative Census Anchoring and GIS Disaggregation

Although prehistoric horizons precede written state administration by more than four millennia, HANDBOOK embeds Regime 1 within a single continuous spatial architecture anchored downstream by subadministrative enumerations. Every modern and historical census polygon is drawn from geoBoundaries administrative vectors [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries] paired with historical provincial boundaries, and disaggregated onto the same 5-arcminute grid via strictly mass-conserving pycnophylactic areal scaling. Across the entire 27-chapter domain, 29 historical provincial enumerations and 2.629 modern subadministrative districts (2.520 matched directly inside the 17 states overlapping this chapter's territorial scope) undergo 65.864 unit-year mass-conservation checks, achieving a 100% pass rate with a global maximum unit relative error of 0,0000058% ($5{,}85 \times 10^{-8}$).

# Testing and Validation

Validation of the prehistoric and Neolithic reconstruction proceeds on three fronts: archaeometric cross-checking of site-level estimates against excavated architectural volumes, internal consistency across kriging diagnostics and mass-conserving spatial aggregation, and subadministrative reconciliation across the modern administrative hierarchy [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries; @BirchChapman2017Estimating; @Palmisano2019Holocene].

At the settlement level, individually evidence-assessed trajectories for 555 sites across 25 modern territories (reconciled alongside 252 excluded duplicate or subordinate candidates out of 807 ledger entries after incorporating NERD, C-Turkey, Palmisano et al. 2021, Titolo and Palmisano 2025 and EES Delta Survey records) were checked against independent architectural, site-area and burial studies. In the southern Levant, Birch-Chapman et al. demonstrate that accounting for open courtyard space, building contemporaneity and roofed floor area places Middle PPNB Beidha around 120 to 240 concurrent inhabitants (assessed here at 235 around 7500BC), while large late PPNB megasites such as 'Ain Ghazal (2,76k) and Basta (2,14k) peaked in the 2k to 3k range around 7000BC [@BirchChapman2017Estimating; @Finlayson2020Beyond]. In central Anatolia, Bogaard et al. and Wright establish that Çatalhöyük East held 3,5k to 8k residents across its 13,5 ha mound during its seventh-millennium peak, closely matching the 4,45k estimate at 6500BC retained here [@Bogaard2017Agricultur; @Wright2013Domesticat]. Across Mesopotamia and Khuzestan, surface sherd scatters and canal alignments confirm that Late Uruk Uruk expanded to 22,4k by 3200BC alongside northern proto-urban centres at Tell Brak (15,9k in 3550BC), Hamoukar (7,55k in 3500BC), Tell al-Hawa (4,15k in 3500BC) and Nineveh (3,78k in 3550BC), Susa (8,15k in 3200BC), Nippur (4,78k), Eridu (4,62k) and Ur (3,84k).

Across the gridded surfaces, all kriging diagnostics clear Gatekeeper sharpness thresholds: raw dimensionless range $\tau_1$ remains between 1,49 and 1,53 across prehistoric horizons, nugget-to-sill ratio stays at 0,04 and uninhabitable desert leakage remains below 1,5% of domain mass. Crucially, the urban mask ensures that modern metropolitan agglomerations (such as Tehran, Giza, Riyadh or Kabul) are excluded from pre-urban back-projection, preventing twentieth-century concrete footprints from distorting Neolithic density surfaces.

Table \ref{tab:subadmin-modern} summarises the 2.520 modern ADM1 and ADM2 divisions across 17 states mapped from geoBoundaries polygons [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries] that complete the downstream spatial anchor. Together with the 20 historical provincial units in Table \ref{tab:subadmin-hist}, these polygons prove mass conservation across every 5-arcminute pixel from 10000BC through 2025, with zero unallocated boundary slivers and zero discrepancies exceeding $5{,}85 \times 10^{-8}$.

# Results

## Regional Population Trajectory from 10000BC to 3200BC

Across the 17 ecological catchments, total population rose from 1,15M in 10000BC to 1,85M in 8000BC (+60,9%), 3,4M in 6000BC (+83,8%), 5,2M in 5000BC (+52,9%), 7,8M in 4000BC (+50%) and 10,6M in 3200BC (+35,9%). Expressed as an annual exponential rate, regional growth averaged 0,024% per year during the Epipalaeolithic-PPNA transition (10000BC to 8000BC), accelerated to 0,03% per year during the PPNB and Early Ceramic expansion (8000BC to 6000BC), peaked at 0,042% per year across the sixth and fifth millennia BC as irrigation agriculture spread across Mesopotamia, Susiana and the Nile (6000BC to 4000BC), and settled at 0,038% per year during the Late Chalcolithic proto-urban surge (4000BC to 3200BC).

Figure \ref{fig:trajectory} and Table \ref{tab:subregion-trajectories} trace that growth across all 17 subregions. Although every catchment expanded over the seven-millennium span, spatial shares shifted markedly toward perennial riverine floodplains once Neolithic farming packages matured and mid-Holocene aridification closed marginal desert corridors.

## Epipalaeolithic and Natufian Levant (10000BC to 8500BC)

During the opening two millennia of the domain, the Levantine Corridor and Jordan Valley formed the densest demographic bridge in Western Asia, rising from 138k inhabitants in 10000BC to 222k in 8000BC. Earlier Epipalaeolithic brush-hut camps in eastern Jordan's Azraq Basin, notably Kharaneh IV around 18000BC, had already shown seasonal multi-band aggregation around perennial wetlands [@Maher2012Twenty]. By the Late Natufian phase (c. 10800BC to 9600BC), communities along the Carmel ridge, the Sea of Galilee and the Bekaa Valley built stone-founded circular huts, limestone bedrock mortars and formal cemeteries at Nahal Ein Gev II, Eynan and Saaïdé II [@Grosman2016Nahal; @Horvath2001Natufian]. Strontium and oxygen isotopic screening across Natufian and PPNA skeletons indicates predominantly local residence patterns, demonstrating that early village formation arose from reduced mobility within established foraging ranges rather than long-range migration [@Santana2021Multi].

Across the Younger Dryas-Holocene boundary around 9700BC to 8500BC, PPNA communities at Jericho, Wadi Faynan 16 (WF16), Netiv Hagdud, Shubayqa 6 in northeast Jordan and Tell Abu Hureyra on the Middle Euphrates built communal storage structures, stone walls and specialised bead-working workshops [@Finlayson2011Architectu; @Thuesen2023Nascent; @Moore1978Neolithic]. Tell Abu Hureyra grew from a 135-person Natufian hamlet in 10000BC to 520 residents in 8500BC and a Late PPNB peak of 3,82k around 7000BC before shifting to smaller Pottery Neolithic phases, while Jericho (peaking at 1,08k in 7500BC), Sha'ar HaGolan (1,38k in 6000BC), Yiftahel and Teleilat Ghassul (1,82k in 4000BC) anchored permanent agricultural nodes along the Jordan Rift [@Yerkes2012Form; @SapirHen2016Human].

## The Fertile Crescent, Anatolia and Cyprus (9500BC to 3200BC)

Between 9000BC and 6000BC, the demographic centre of gravity broadened from the southern Levant across northern Syria, southeastern Anatolia, the Anatolian Plateau and Cyprus. Along the Upper Euphrates and Tigris foothills, Pre-Pottery Neolithic communities erected circular monumental enclosures carved with T-shaped limestone pillars at Göbekli Tepe and Karahan Tepe in an open pistachio-oak parkland steppe [@Biltekin2024Exploring; @Sweatman2024Representa]. At nearby Çayönü Tepesi on the Ergani plain, continuous stratigraphic layers trace the architectural shift from round wattle-and-daub huts through grill-plan, channelled and cell-plan stone foundations across its 3,8 ha mound, reaching an Aceramic peak of 780 inhabitants around 7500BC alongside Göbekli Tepe (640 in 9000BC) and Körtik Tepe (245 in 9500BC).

In the middle and late PPNB (8500BC to 6800BC), demographic expansion across the southern Levant and northern Syria produced megasites along springs and wadi confluences: 'Ain Ghazal, Basta, Beidha, Ghwair I, Ba'ja, Yiftahel and Tell Qarassa [@BirchChapman2017Estimating; @Balbo2012Squaring; @Benz2019Burying; @Slon2014Plastered; @Woodman2005Ground]. Intensive caprine management replaced wild gazelle hunting as the primary meat source [@Munro2018Emergence; @SapirHen2016Human], while rectangular mudbrick houses allowed dense multi-room compounds [@Balbo2012Squaring; @Kadowaki2012Household]. Along the Mediterranean littoral, seafarers colonised Cyprus as early as 10000BC to 8500BC at Aetokremnos and Klimonas, establishing round-house farming villages at Shillourokambos (195 in 7500BC), Khirokitia (450 in 6000BC), Ayios Epiktitos-Vrysi and Kissonerga-Mosphilia (680 in 3200BC); the island's catchments grew from 9,2k in 10000BC to 84,8k by 3200BC. Coastal Levantine sites also faced acute marine hazards, including a seventh-millennium mega-tsunami recorded at Tel Dor along the Carmel coast [@Shtienberg2020Neolithic]. Over the full Holocene span, summed radiocarbon curves across the Levant confirm rapid PPNB expansion followed by localised seventh-millennium restructuring and steady Chalcolithic recovery, carrying the Levantine Corridor to 408k in 6000BC and 1,27M in 3200BC [@Palmisano2019Holocene; @Borrell2015Synchronou].

Across the Taurus Mountains, the Anatolian Plateau and Coasts expanded from 149,5k in 10000BC to 442k in 6000BC and 1,38M by 3200BC. On the Konya Plain, Çatalhöyük East rose to 4,45k residents around 6500BC (alongside earlier Cappadocian Aşıklı Höyük at 980 in 7500BC) without centralised streets or monumental palaces, relying on household-level storage bins, diversified cereal-pulse cropping, sheep herding and grinding-stone food processing [@Bogaard2017Agricultur; @Wright2013Domesticat; @Coulardeau2023Sedentaris]. Further west and south, Aegean, Marmara, Cilician and Lake District farming centres at Ulucak Höyük (540), Hacılar (460), Ilıpınar (420), Mersin-Yumuktepe (1,16k), Domuztepe (1,76k) and Late Chalcolithic Arslantepe (1,68k) linked central Anatolian ceramic traditions to early seaborne and overland farming dispersals into southeastern Europe after 6500BC [@Budja2009Early].

## Mesopotamia and the Tigris-Euphrates Alluvium

While piedmont rain-fed villages in northern Iraq and northern Syria (Tell Hassuna, Tepe Gawra, Tell Sabi Abyad, Tell Halaf and Choga Mami) prospered during the sixth millennium BC, fifth- and fourth-millennium urbanisation surged across both Upper Mesopotamia and the southern alluvial delta.

Canal irrigation along anastomosing Euphrates and Tigris channels transformed seasonally flooded silt plains into high-yielding barley and date-palm estates. The Tigris-Euphrates Alluvial Basin grew from 172,5k in 10000BC and 277,5k in 8000BC to 510k in 6000BC, 780k in 5000BC, 1,17M in 4000BC and 1,59M by 3200BC.

By the Late Chalcolithic and Late Uruk horizons, Ubaid temple-towns had evolved into the earliest true cities: Uruk surged to 22,4k inhabitants by 3200BC—over five times Çatalhöyük's peak—while northern centres at Tell Brak (15,9k in 3550BC; 12,2k in 3200BC), Hamoukar (7,55k; 5,35k), Tell al-Hawa (4,15k) and Nineveh (3,78k) reached comparable complexity across the Khabur and Upper Tigris. Southern temple-towns at Nippur (4,78k), Eridu (4,62k) and Ur (3,84k) anchored dense canal hierarchies alongside earlier Ubaid centres like Tell Oueili.

## Predynastic Nile Valley, Delta and Western Oases

In 10000BC, the Nile Valley, Delta and Western Oases already held an estimated 184k fisher-foragers along seasonal river levees, Fayum lake margins and Saharan springs. Growth proceeded slowly through the Early Holocene (296k in 8000BC) until southwest Asian emmer wheat, barley, sheep and goats entered Lower Egypt and the Fayum around 5500BC to 5000BC.

As the Eastern Sahara desiccated after 5300BC, mobile cattle herders from Nabta Playa, Bir Kiseiba and the Western Oases converged on the Nile floodplain. By 6000BC the catchment held 544k inhabitants; by 5000BC it reached 832k; by 4000BC, during the flourishing of Merimde Beni Salama (1,06k in 4500BC), Maadi (1,19k in 3500BC), El-Badari and Naqada I-II, numbers climbed to 1,25M.

By 3200BC, on the threshold of Upper and Lower Egyptian political unification, the Nile basin carried 1,7M inhabitants, anchored by 15 individually evidence-assessed excavated and surveyed sites across Egypt spanning the Western Oases to the Delta. Leading terminal Predynastic centres included Hierakonpolis (6,35k) and Naqada (4,15k) in Upper Egypt alongside Buto (2,16k) in the northwestern Delta, linked to earlier lakeside and oasis stations at Kom W, Nabta Playa, Dakhla Oasis and Siwa Oasis.

## Zagros Piedmont, Iranian Plateau and Transcaucasia

East of Mesopotamia, the Zagros Piedmont, Susiana and Fars grew from 115k in 10000BC to 185k in 8000BC, 340k in 6000BC, 520k in 5000BC, 780k in 4000BC and 1,06M in 3200BC. Early goat herding and wild-cereal collection at highland camps such as Ganj Dareh gave way to lowland irrigation settlements on the Deh Luran, Susiana and Fars plains (Ali Kosh, Chogha Mish at 2,48k in 3500BC, Tall-e Bakun and Tol-e Nurabad), where Susa surged to 8,15k inhabitants by 3200BC.

Beyond the Zagros crest, the Iranian Plateau and Khorasan rose from 57,5k in 10000BC to 170k in 6000BC and 530k in 3200BC across oasis tells including Yanik Tepe near Lake Urmia (950), Tepe Zagheh on the Qazvin plain (680), Sang-e Chakhmaq (670), Tepe Sialk near Kashan (2,34k), Tepe Hissar near Damghan (2,25k), Tal-i Iblis (590) and Tepe Yahya (790).

Northward across the Aras and Kura rivers, Transcaucasia and the Kura-Aras Basin expanded from 46k in 10000BC to 136k in 6000BC and 424k in 3200BC. Early farming anchored itself in Shulaveri-Shomu circular-mudbrick villages at Shulaveris Gora (190), Göytepe (345) and Aknashen (155) before shifting toward Chalcolithic and Early Kura-Aras settlements including Mentesh Tepe (390) and Ovçular Tepesi (720 in 3500BC, 640 in 3200BC).

## Early Afghanistan, Arabian Wadis and Capsian North Africa

At the eastern edge of the domain, early hunter-gatherers and Neolithic pastoralists occupied the foothills of the Hindu Kush and the Sistan-Helmand basin. The Hindu Kush and Bactrian Foothills rose from 34,5k in 10000BC to 102k in 6000BC and 318k in 3200BC, while the Helmand and Sistan Basin rose from 17,3k to 159k over the same interval.

Early occupation in northern limestone caves and alluvial-fan camps such as Aq Kupruk, Kara Kamar, Tashkurgan 40 and Darra-i Kur gave way during the fourth millennium to mounded Helmand-Sistan proto-urban centres at Shahr-i Sokhta (2,45k upon foundation in 3200BC) and Mundigak (1,68k in 3200BC), flanked by Chalcolithic tells at Said Qala Tepe (340), Deh Morasi Ghundai (245) and Gardan Reg (230).

Across the southern and western drylands, Holocene pluvial phases enabled widespread mid-Holocene habitation before aridification checked growth. In North Africa, the Maghreb Tell and Atlas Basins grew from 92k in 10000BC to 272k in 6000BC and 848k in 3200BC across Capsian *escargotières* and Neolithic cave-and-terrace settlements such as Medjez II (135), El-Mekta (115), Ifri Oudadane (95), Gueldaman (90), Columnata (85), Kehf el-Baroud (85) and Kef Zoura D (65), while the Tripolitania and Cyrenaica Coast expanded from 23k in 10000BC to 68k in 6000BC and 212k in 3200BC around Haua Fteah (130), Shakshuk (80) and Abiar Miggi (60).

Saharan and Fezzan Pluvial Basins expanded from 28,8k in 10000BC to 85k in 6000BC and 265k in 3200BC across pastoralist camps at Takarkori, Hassi Mouillah, Amekni, Tin Hanakaten and Uan Afuda, while Atlantic Sahara Wadis supported 2,3k to 21,2k coastal and wadi foragers at Izriten, Oued Chebeika, Tifariti and Ashash. On the Arabian Peninsula, recent excavations at Al Uyaynah in Tabuk, Al-Ula, Shuwaymis and Jebel Oraf in the Jubbah oasis confirm Pre-Pottery Neolithic B-derived and pastoralist incursions into the Nefud Desert during the Early Holocene wet phase [@Crassard2013Beyond; @Alasmari2026Results; @Birkenfeld2020Hunting].

Monsoon-fed highland villages in Yemen and Asir (40,3k in 10000BC to 371k in 3200BC, including Jubabat al-Juruf, Wadi at-Tayyilah 3 and Al-Sihi) and coastal shell-midden settlements in Oman, the Gulf Coast and Hadramawt (23k to 212k, led by Dosariyah at 235 and Ra's al-Hamra at 210 alongside As-Sabiyah, Marawah and Suwayh), together with Interior Arabian Wadis and Nefud (17,3k to 159k), brought total Arabian population from 80,5k in 10000BC to 742k by 3200BC.

## Spatial Intensity and Settlement Hierarchy

<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_handbook/1.0-prehistoric-neolithic-mena-iran-afghanistan/fig3_prehistoric_neolithic_mena_iran_afghanistan_density.png" alt="fig:density" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 3.</span> Kriged Late Neolithic and Chalcolithic site intensity surface (left) and mean catchment density in 3200BC across leading basins (right).</figcaption>
</figure>

Figure \ref{fig:density} illustrates the continuous kriged Late Neolithic-Chalcolithic surface alongside mean regional densities in 3200BC. Density contrasts were already stark: narrow irrigated or Mediterranean corridors such as the Levantine Corridor, the Nile Valley-Delta and Cyprus achieved high per-kilometre concentrations, whereas vast desert-basin catchments in the Sahara and interior Arabia remained thinly peopled even during humid intervals.

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:settlements">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_handbook/1.0-prehistoric-neolithic-mena-iran-afghanistan/fig4_prehistoric_neolithic_mena_iran_afghanistan_settlements.png" alt="fig:settlements" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 4.</span> Rank-size distribution across 555 individually evidence-assessed settlements (Zipf slope 0,9, R² = 0,92) (left) and the twelve largest urban and proto-urban mounds between 10000BC and 3200BC (right).</figcaption>
</figure>

Across all 555 individually evidence-assessed settlements, the peak-population rank-size curve (Figure \ref{fig:settlements}) yields a well-graded power-law Zipf exponent ($\alpha = 0,90$, $R^2 = 0,92$, unrounded $\alpha = 0,895$), reflecting the continuous hierarchy linking a broad base of small Epipalaeolithic camps and Neolithic villages (50 to 1k residents) to late fourth-millennium proto-urban centres led by Uruk (22,4k), Tell Brak (15,9k), Susa (8,15k), Hamoukar (7,55k) and Hierakonpolis (6,35k) above secondary riverine and plateau towns such as Nippur (4,78k), Eridu (4,62k), Çatalhöyük (4,45k), Tell al-Hawa (4,15k), Naqada (4,15k), Ur (3,84k) and Tell Abu Hureyra (3,82k).

# Limitations

Prehistoric demographic reconstruction across a landmass stretching from the Atlantic Sahara to the Hindu Kush faces four structural constraints. First, archaeological survey intensity varies by an order of magnitude across constituent countries: Israel, Palestine, Jordan, Lebanon, Cyprus, western Syria and central Anatolia possess dense foot-survey coverage and large radiocarbon inventories, whereas interior Libya, Atlantic Morocco, highland Yemen and Afghanistan remain sparsely surveyed outside major oasis basins or rescue corridors. Kriging over Voronoi catchments corrects for spatial clustering where surveys exist, yet cannot invent undocumented sites in unwalked mountain valleys or sand seas.

Second, alluvial aggradation and coastal submergence selectively erase early sites. Across the lower Tigris-Euphrates delta and the Nile Delta, several metres of post-Neolithic river silt bury Epipalaeolithic and early Neolithic occupations beneath modern water tables, while post-glacial Mediterranean sea-level rise drowned coastal camps older than 6000BC. Conversely, stone-built tells on dry limestone plateaus remain visible on satellite imagery for millennia, creating a taphonomic bias toward upland settlements.

Third, inferring living population from excavated site area or tell volume introduces a 20% to 35% margin of uncertainty around household size, open-courtyard ratios and phase contemporaneity [@BirchChapman2017Estimating; @Kadowaki2012Household]. Many large PPNB and Chalcolithic mounds shifted habitation laterally across centuries rather than packing every hectare simultaneously.

Fourth, exact chronological synchronisation between Near Eastern ceramic phases, Egyptian predynastic horizons, Iranian plateau sequences and Capsian North Africa remains imprecise prior to 4000BC where radiocarbon calibration plateaux flatten dates. Regional totals reported at 10000BC, 8000BC, 6000BC, 5000BC, 4000BC and 3200BC should therefore be read as smoothed centennial envelopes rather than single-year censuses.

# Conclusion

Between 10000BC and 3200BC, the territories covered by HANDBOOK moved from dispersed Epipalaeolithic foraging bands numbering 1,15M inhabitants to an interconnected agrarian and pastoral world of 10,6M inhabitants. Growth was neither instantaneous nor confined to one river valley: Natufian and PPNA aggregation in the Levant, Anatolian village consolidation at Çatalhöyük and Çayönü, Zagros goat domestication, Saharan-Arabian wet-phase pastoralism and Transcaucasian foothill farming all contributed before fifth- and fourth-millennium irrigation turned the Nile Valley (1,7M) and the Tigris-Euphrates Basin (1,59M) into the demographic pillars of the ancient Near East. Combining site-based architectural multipliers with metric-isotropic radial interpolation, non-stationary Matérn kriging and mass-conserving subadministrative anchoring ensures that these prehistoric baselines connect cleanly to the dynastic, classical and modern demographic series explored in subsequent chapters.

## Chronological Anchoring of Catchment Totals

Between 10000BC and 3200BC, catchment estimates are reported at six primary horizons matching the regional archaeological and radiocarbon chronology: 10000BC (Late Natufian and Younger Dryas recovery), 8000BC (PPNB expansion), 6000BC (Ceramic Neolithic and Holocene Optimum), 5000BC (Halaf-Ubaid and early Nile farming), 4000BC (Uruk and Naqada consolidation) and 3200BC (terminal Chalcolithic threshold prior to dynastic state formation).

Each regional table and gridded surface preserves exact additive consistency between the 17 catchment totals and the pan-domain headline series (1,15M in 10000BC rising to 10,6M in 3200BC), establishing an unbroken baseline for the Bronze Age chapters that follow.
